added.name: Christian Whitmer
added.desc: Book of Mormon — Christian Whitmer is one of the eight signatories of the Testimony of Eight Witnesses. Only that signatory role is asserted here; the shared surname does not by itself make him kin to the other Whitmers. See also: “Testimony of Eight Witnesses”.

added.name: Jacob Whitmer
added.desc: Book of Mormon — Jacob Whitmer is one of the eight signatories of the Testimony of Eight Witnesses. Only that signatory role is asserted here; the shared surname does not by itself make him kin to the other Whitmers. See also: “Testimony of Eight Witnesses”.

added.name: Joseph Smith—History: the Smith family
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Joseph Smith—History 1:3–4 and 7: Joseph names his father, Joseph Smith Sr., and his mother, Lucy Smith, formerly Mack, a daughter of Solomon Mack. The children named are Alvin, Hyrum, Joseph, Samuel Harrison, William, Don Carlos, Sophronia, Catherine and Lucy; Lucy the mother and Lucy the daughter are two people. Verse 7 reports Presbyterian membership for his mother, Hyrum, Samuel Harrison and Sophronia, not for the whole family. These are the narrator’s reported relationships, not corroborated civil records. See also: “Alvin in Joseph Smith's family account”, “Joseph Smith Sr.”, “Hyrum Smith”, “Samuel H. Smith”.

added.name: Joseph Smith—History: Stoal, Hale and Tarbill
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Joseph Smith—History 1:56–58: Joseph works for Josiah Stoal (the account’s spelling), who employs him in a search for a silver mine in Harmony; the reported search fails. Joseph boards with Isaac Hale, whose daughter is Emma. Joseph and Emma are reported married on January 18, 1827, at the house of Squire Tarbill in South Bainbridge; Tarbill is given no first name here. The failed mine search is kept as reported. See also: “Emma Smith”, “Joseph Smith—History: family moves, marriage and translation”.

added.name: Joseph Smith—History: Harris’s trip, as relayed
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Joseph Smith—History 1:61–65: Martin Harris gives Joseph financial help with his move, and separately carries copied characters to New York City. Professor Charles Anthon and Dr. Mitchell (no first name given) appear in Harris’s account as Joseph relays it; the reported certification is not presented as an independently verified statement by either man. Joseph is not routed along Harris’s trip. See also: “Martin Harris”.

added.name: Joseph Smith—History: Moroni, the plates and the objects
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Joseph Smith—History 1:30–54 and 59–60: Moroni is the named heavenly messenger in the account. The plates, the Urim and Thummim, the breastplate, the stone box, the annual visits to the hill and the eventual return of the plates to the messenger are distinct reported objects and episodes; none is drawn as a separate pin. Receiving the plates on September 22, 1827 is not the first, 1823 hill visit, and the account’s “until this day” 1838 narration date is not the date of the return. See also: “Receiving the plates”, “Hill near Manchester (PGP)”.

added.name: Joseph Smith—History: scribe, baptism and priesthood
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Joseph Smith—History 1:66–75: Oliver Cowdery serves as Joseph’s scribe. Joseph baptizes Oliver and Oliver baptizes Joseph. In the account John the Baptist confers the Aaronic Priesthood on both; Peter, James and John are named as the authorities directing him, not as appearing in this baptism scene. Aaron, Levi and Melchizedek appear in priesthood terms, not as people present. Joseph’s promised office of first elder and Oliver’s of second elder are future offices, not a church already organized in May 1829. See also: “Reported baptisms”, “Susquehanna River baptism setting”, “Oliver Cowdery”.

added.name: Joseph Smith—History: people quoted or compared
added.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Joseph Smith—History 1:11, 24, 36–41 and 69–72: James (the quoted epistle), Paul and King Agrippa (a comparison), Malachi, Isaiah, Joel and Elijah (quoted or anticipated prophecy), and Christ and divine titles are text references with the roles those verses give them. No 1820s meeting with any of them is created. The appended 1834 Cowdery reminiscence, which separately names Mormon, Moroni and the seed of Jacob, is its own card. See also: “Oliver Cowdery’s 1834 account, appended”.

before.name: Seth’s line to Noah: who is who
before.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Moses 6:2–25 and 8:5–12 give the parent chain Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech and Noah; ages are the account’s own reported figures, not dates. Cainan the person is distinct from the land of Cainan, and this Enos is not the Book of Mormon writer. Mahijah questions Enoch (Moses 6:40); Mahujah is a place (Moses 7:2). The two similar names are not identified with each other. See also: “Seth’s line: Adam to Methuselah”, “Lamech, Noah and Noah’s sons”, “Land of Cainan”, “Mahujah”.

after.name: Seth’s line to Noah: who is who
after.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Moses 6:2–25 and 8:5–12 give the parent chain Seth, Enos, Cainan, Mahalaleel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech and Noah. The account reports each father’s age when the named son is born: Adam 130 at Seth (6:10), Seth 105 at Enos (6:13), Enos 90 at Cainan (6:17), Cainan 70 at Mahalaleel (6:19), Mahalaleel 65 at Jared (6:20), Jared 162 at Enoch (6:21), Enoch 65 at Methuselah (6:25), Methuselah 187 at Lamech (8:5) and Lamech 182 at Noah (8:8–9). These are the account’s own reported ages, not independently established dates, and no calendar years are derived from them. Cainan the person is distinct from the land of Cainan, and this Enos is not the Book of Mormon writer. Mahijah questions Enoch (Moses 6:40); Mahujah is a place (Moses 7:2). The two similar names are not identified with each other. See also: “Seth’s line: Adam to Methuselah”, “Lamech, Noah and Noah’s sons”, “Land of Cainan”, “Mahujah”.

before.name: Abraham’s family in Abraham 2
before.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Abraham 2:1–4: Haran and Nahor are Abraham’s brothers; Milcah is Haran’s daughter and Nahor’s wife; Terah is Abraham’s father and Sarai his wife; Lot is Abraham’s nephew, and Lot’s wife is not named. The passage calls Lot “my brother’s son” without naming that brother, so Abraham’s account alone does not make Haran Lot’s father. Haran the brother is not the city of Haran. See also: “Abraham’s covenant and household”, “Haran (Genesis)”.

after.name: Abraham’s family in Abraham 2
after.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Abraham 2:1–4: Haran and Nahor are Abraham’s brothers; Milcah is Haran’s daughter and Nahor’s wife; Terah is Abraham’s father; Sarai is Abraham’s wife; Lot is Abraham’s nephew, and Lot’s wife is not named. The passage calls Lot “my brother’s son” without naming that brother, so Abraham’s account alone does not make Haran Lot’s father. Haran the brother is not the city of Haran. See also: “Abraham’s covenant and household”, “Haran (Genesis)”.

before.name: Facsimile vocabulary, as published
before.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Facsimile 2, explanation, figures 1–5, names Oliblish, Enish-go-on-dosh, Jah-oh-eh, Kae-e-vanrash, Floeese, Kli-flos-is-es and Hah-ko-kau-beam; Facsimile 1, explanation, figure 12, names Raukeeyang, Shaumau and Shaumahyeem. Each term’s role or gloss is the one its caption gives (linked). All are attributed interpretation vocabulary, not coordinates, authenticated Egyptian translations or measured astronomical bodies. Where a shared sun or moon gloss relates two terms, such as Floeese and Olea or Enish-go-on-dosh and Shinehah, that gloss is the only basis for relating them; they are not otherwise merged. See also: “Facsimile explanations as attributed interpretation”, “Facsimile 2: published explanation”.

after.name: Facsimile vocabulary, as published
after.desc: Pearl of Great Price — Facsimile 2, explanation, figures 1–5, names Oliblish, Enish-go-on-dosh, Jah-oh-eh, Kae-e-vanrash, Floeese, Kli-flos-is-es and Hah-ko-kau-beam; Facsimile 1, explanation, figure 12, names Raukeeyang, Shaumau and Shaumahyeem. In the published explanations, Oliblish is a governing creation next to Kolob; Jah-oh-eh names Earth. Enish-go-on-dosh is associated with the Sun. Kae-e-vanrash is a governing power; Floeese denotes the Moon. Kli-flos-is-es and Hah-ko-kau-beam name the stars represented by figures 22 and 23. Raukeeyang denotes expanse or firmament; the explanation relates it here to Shaumau, height or heavens, and to Shaumahyeem. Each term’s role or gloss is the one its caption gives (linked); this is not a complete glossary. All are attributed interpretation vocabulary, not coordinates, authenticated Egyptian translations or measured astronomical bodies. Where a shared sun or moon gloss relates two terms, such as Floeese and Olea or Enish-go-on-dosh and Shinehah, that gloss is the only basis for relating them; they are not otherwise merged. See also: “Facsimile explanations as attributed interpretation”, “Facsimile 2: published explanation”.

before.name: Book of Mormon publication setting
before.desc: The edition identifies Palmyra as the first English publication setting in 1830 and Salt Lake City as the publisher’s location.

after.name: Book of Mormon publication setting
after.desc: The edition identifies Palmyra as the first English publication setting in 1830 and Salt Lake City as the publisher’s location. This is the same Palmyra as the map’s Palmyra marker, here as a neutral publication setting with the year only; the more precise month of publication belongs to the separately sourced publication history in a later layer. Salt Lake City as the publisher’s location is not the 1847 arrival in the valley.

before.name: Book of Mormon title and attributed record
before.desc: The title presents the work as an abridgment associated with Mormon and Moroni, including a Jaredite record, addressed to Lamanites, Jews and Gentiles.

after.name: Book of Mormon title and attributed record
after.desc: The title presents the work as an abridgment associated with Mormon and Moroni, including a Jaredite record, addressed to Lamanites, Jews and Gentiles. Abridging, sealing up and addressing are kept as distinct relations, not one act. Joseph Smith Jr. is credited as translator. The title supplies no site and no calendar date. See also: “Keepers of the records: Nephi to Moroni”.

before.name: Book of Mormon introduction
before.desc: The Church introduction describes the Lamanites as among the ancestors of American Indians and presents Christ’s Nephite ministry as the book’s central event.

after.name: Book of Mormon introduction
after.desc: The Church introduction describes the Lamanites as among the ancestors of American Indians and presents Christ’s Nephite ministry as the book’s central event. This is official editorial teaching, attributed to the introduction; it is not a DNA finding and not a claim that all Indigenous ancestry comes from one group. The introduction names Cumorah in its account of the plates; that editorial mention is not used to fix a modern location for the battle in Mormon 6. See also: “Cumorah / Ramah”.

before.name: Testimony of Three Witnesses
before.desc: Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer and Martin Harris testify that an angel showed them the plates and that a divine voice affirmed the translation.

after.name: Testimony of Three Witnesses
after.desc: Oliver Cowdery, David Whitmer and Martin Harris testify that an angel showed them the plates and that a divine voice affirmed the translation. Each signs the printed testimony and reports seeing; this is participant testimony as printed. The page gives no venue and no day, so no event is pinned. Their names are visible from the Book of Mormon layer; relationships reported in later works stay in those layers, and no surname alone shows kinship.

before.name: Testimony of Eight Witnesses
before.desc: Eight named witnesses (Christian Whitmer, Jacob Whitmer, Peter Whitmer Jr., John Whitmer, Hiram Page, Joseph Smith Sr., Hyrum Smith and Samuel H. Smith) testify that Joseph Smith showed them plates, which they handled and described as having the appearance of gold.

after.name: Testimony of Eight Witnesses
after.desc: Eight named witnesses (Christian Whitmer, Jacob Whitmer, Peter Whitmer Jr., John Whitmer, Hiram Page, Joseph Smith Sr., Hyrum Smith and Samuel H. Smith) testify that Joseph Smith showed them plates, which they handled and described as having the appearance of gold. This is printed testimony; no independent metallurgical test is reported. No date or venue is inferred. Only the signatory role is asserted here: shared surnames do not establish kinship, and family relationships reported in later works stay in those layers. See also: “Christian Whitmer”, “Jacob Whitmer”.

before.name: Joseph Smith’s testimony of the plates
before.desc: Smith recounts Moroni’s 1823 visits, repeated annual instruction, receipt of the plates on September 22, 1827 and later return to the messenger.

src.t: Testimony of the Prophet Joseph Smith

after.name: Joseph Smith’s testimony of the plates
after.desc: Smith recounts Moroni’s 1823 visits, repeated annual instruction, receipt of the plates on September 22, 1827 and later return to the messenger. This is a first-person religious narrative and the Book of Mormon front-matter view of the same reported episodes told in Joseph Smith’s longer history, not additional visits or a second plates event. Collapsing in the field, the instruction that follows and the visit to the hill stay distinct actions, kept to the account; no roads are drawn. The account places the hill near Manchester but gives no survey coordinate, and neither an editorial Cumorah label nor a modern monument settles where Mormon 6’s battle took place. May 2, 1838 is the account’s stated reporting vantage, not the date the plates were returned.

src.t: Testimony of the Prophet Joseph Smith

before.name: Book of Mormon record explanation
before.desc: The edition distinguishes the small and large plates of Nephi, Mormon’s abridgment, Ether’s record and the brass plates.

src.t: Brief explanation about the Book of Mormon

after.name: Book of Mormon record explanation
after.desc: The edition distinguishes the small and large plates of Nephi, Mormon’s abridgment, Ether’s record and the brass plates. This is an editorial explanation of textual provenance, not an archaeological recovery claim, and its date of about 421 is the edition’s editorial attribution. It identifies the nonitalic narrative introductions and the original title as sacred text, and the italic chapter headings as study helps. No journey is drawn. See also: “Keepers of the small plates”.

src.t: Brief explanation about the Book of Mormon

before.name: Doctrine and Covenants collection history
before.desc: The introduction traces manuscript copying, interrupted Missouri printing in 1833 and later publication and revision of the collection.

after.name: Doctrine and Covenants collection history
after.desc: The introduction traces manuscript copying, interrupted Missouri printing in 1833 and later publication and revision of the collection. This is the Church’s documentary synthesis. The 1835 printed testimony naming the Twelve and its account of an earlier 1831 testimony are kept as distinct documentary contexts. The Lectures on Faith, omitted from the 1921 edition, are historical context, not a current unit of the canon. The collection-level description of modern origin does not erase section 7’s attribution as a translated record. See also: “Independence”, “Kirtland Temple”.

before.name: Pearl of Great Price collection history
before.desc: The introduction describes Franklin D. Richards’s 1851 collection, 1880 canonization and later changes to its contents.

after.name: Pearl of Great Price collection history
after.desc: The introduction describes Franklin D. Richards’s 1851 collection, 1880 canonization and later changes to its contents. It names Franklin D. Richards as compiler and as president of the British Mission. Sections 137 and 138 were added to the Pearl of Great Price in 1976 and transferred to the Doctrine and Covenants in 1979; their inclusion in the 1981 edition of the Doctrine and Covenants is a separate publication milestone. The five component descriptions are the existing Pearl of Great Price cards. Nauvoo periodical publication dates do not date Abraham’s narrated journey.
